gam-cs-cp-001-q1.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p2 states the system drops whichever record has gone longest without being asked for, and that a hit counts as an asking. Initial recency order (oldest first): P, Q, R. The request for Q is a hit, so Q is refreshed and the order becomes P (oldest), R, Q. The request for S is a miss; p1 says on a miss the record is fetched and placed in the cache, and if the cache is full one record must be dropped. The cache holds three and is full, so option d is excluded. The least-recently-asked record is P. Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): determinable without the pack (would have chosen "a", confidence medium) — The stem supplies the full recency order (R most recent, then Q, P longest ago), the hit on Q refreshes Q, and the cache is full at three. Under the two conventional policies a pack titled 'a cache and its replacement policy' would state — LRU or FIFO — P is evicted either way; only MRU or a tie-broken LFU would differ, and neither is a default a reader would assume. Option d is excluded because the cache already holds three of three.

adjudicator.model: Claude Opus 5 (full ablation) + Claude Opus 5 (blind re-answer)

evidence.ablationLeakDetail: q2's correct option (fetch on a miss and make room if the cache is full) rules out q1's option d, which claims S can be admitted without an eviction. It does not touch the P/Q/R choice, so it removes one of four rather than deciding the item.

gam-cs-cp-001-q2.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p1: 'otherwise it is a miss, the record is fetched and placed in the cache, and if the cache is full one record must be dropped to make room.' Option b restates exactly that. a, c and d contradict it (nothing in the pack supports refusal, or a second-request threshold). Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): determinable without the pack (would have chosen "b", confidence high) — Demand-fill with eviction is the ordinary meaning of a cache; a leaves the cache permanently cold, c is not a behaviour any cache has, and d is a second-chance admission policy the stem gives no reason to expect.

evidence.ablationLeakDetail: STEM RESTATES ANOTHER'S ANSWER. q1's stem asserts, as given fact, that on a request for S (a record not in the cache) a record 'is dropped to make room for S'. That is q2's option b almost word for word, and it is incompatible with a (cache left as it was), c (request refused) and d (cached only on second request). A candidate who reads q1 first can answer q2 without the source at all. The item is independently determinable from domain knowledge, but the coupling itself is total.

gam-cs-cp-001-q3.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p1 defines the hit rate as the share of requests that are hits, i.e. requests met without going to the slow store. Table t1: index 97, document 61, thumbnail 88, session 79 per cent. The smallest is the document cache at 61 per cent. Records held (512) is a distractor column and is not what is asked. Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): not-determinable without the pack (would have chosen "b", confidence low) — Pure table lookup: 'smallest share met without going to the slow store' is the lowest hit rate among four named caches, and no stem or option carries a figure. The choice of document cache is a guess from the general expectation that a long-tail document working set caches worse than indexes, thumbnails or sessions; it is not evidence.

gam-cs-cp-001-q4.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p3: 'A hit rate is a property of the pairing of a cache with the pattern of requests it happens to meet... they are not a ranking of the caches in themselves.' gam-econ-pt-001-q1.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p3: a part tonne is rounded up before the rate is applied, so 120.4 tonnes becomes 121 tonnes. t1: general cargo is 4 euros per tonne, so 121 x 4 = 484 euros. p2: the class minimum (200 euros) applies only where the tonnage fee falls below it; 484 > 200, so the tonnage fee stands. The distractors are 120.4 x 4 = 481.60 (no rounding) and 120 x 4 = 480 (rounding down). Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): not-determinable without the pack (would have chosen "d", confidence low) — The option set recovers the general rate as 4 euros per tonne (480 = 120 x 4, 481.60 = 120.4 x 4, 484 = 121 x 4), and 200 is almost certainly the class minimum, which does not bind here. What it cannot recover is the rounding convention the tariff states — exact tonnage, nearest tonne, or per commenced tonne — and that convention is the whole content of the item. 484 is a lean on the ground that 120.4 was chosen to make a rounding rule bite, not a determination.

gam-ns-lox-001-q1.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p3: a trout needs at least 5 mg per litre. Figure 1 summer series: 4 m = 9.0, 6 m = 8.5, 8 m = 4.0. Only eight metres falls below 5 mg/l (4.0 < 5), so c, and d is excluded. The winter series (about 10.6 at 8 m) is not what is asked. Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): determinable without the pack (would have chosen "c", confidence medium) — Ordinary limnology: in a summer-stratified lake, oxygen is depleted below the thermocline, so the deepest listed depth is the one that fails a trout threshold. The threshold value and the figure's actual curve are the source's to supply, and if the thermocline sits shallow both six and eight metres could qualify, so this is a knowledge-led read rather than a certainty.

Together they make a summer depth gradient certain from the siblings alone, which argues strongly against q1's option d ('none of the depths shown') and points the answer to the deepest depth. Not decisive: a gradient need not cross the trout threshold anywhere.

gam-ns-lox-001-q2.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p1 defines it: 'the thermocline, a band of depth across which the temperature falls sharply'. a (light), c (oxygen threshold) and d (breakdown layer) each borrow other ideas from p1 but none is the definition given. Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): determinable without the pack (would have chosen "b", confidence high) — Standard definition — the thermocline is a band of steep temperature change with depth. a describes the aphotic zone, c redefines it by oxygen, d describes benthic decomposition.

gam-ns-lox-001-q3.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): p2: 'In winter the surface water cools until it is no denser than the water beneath, the lake turns over from top to bottom, and oxygen is carried down with it, so a winter profile is close to uniform at every depth.' That is option c. Option a states a real-world fact about cold water and oxygen solubility that this pack never asserts, and it would not by itself explain uniformity with depth; b and d are not in the text (d also contradicts p1/p2). Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): determinable without the pack (would have chosen "c", confidence high) — Autumn cooling drives turnover, and it is the mixing that carries oxygen to depth. a states a true fact (cold water holds more oxygen) that does not explain uniformity with depth, b denies a process rather than supplying one, d misuses the thermocline.

Note that the item largely discloses its own answer: option b states the sampling hour, which is the fact the source has to supply. c is scientifically not silly — below the thermocline diel variation is small — but it changes the measurement instead of reconciling it.

gam-cs-cp-001-q1.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): Block p2 states the policy: drop whichever record has gone longest without being asked for, and a hit counts as an asking that refreshes the record. Traced step by step: initial last-asked order is P (longest ago), then Q, then R (most recent). The request for Q is a hit (p1: the record is already in the cache), so Q moves to the most recent position, leaving order P oldest, then R, then Q. The request for S is a miss; the cache holds three records and is full, so per p1 one record must be dropped, and per p2 that is the one longest without being asked for, namely P. Option d fails because the hit on Q frees no space — S is still a miss into a full cache. Options b and c are the two records refreshed most recently. Worth flagging for the item author: the hit rule in p2 is not load-bearing here, because P is the least recently used both with and without the refresh of Q, so a candidate who ignores the 'a hit counts as an asking' sentence still lands on the keyed answer. That is a discrimination weakness, not an ambiguity. Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): determinable without the pack (would have chosen "a", confidence medium) — The stem supplies the only state a replacement decision needs — a full three-record cache and a recency ordering (P oldest, then Q, then R), refreshed by the hit on Q. Option d is self-defeating: a hit on Q frees nothing, and the cache is already full, so something must go. Of the standard policies, least-recently-used and any insertion-order/FIFO reading both evict P; only most-recently-used would evict Q, and the stem's decision to state last-asked order (rather than insertion order) signals a recency policy. The residual risk is that the source names an unusual policy — the phrase 'according to the policy' points at a rule the pack states — but no plausible documented policy makes R the victim, so ordinary domain knowledge reaches P without the pack. Note this is genuine standard-CS knowledge, not leakage: the pack is doing little work here beyond naming the policy.

gam-cs-cp-001-q1.rationale: Blind re-answer (Claude Opus 5, confidence high): Traced step by step against p2 only. Initial state, ordered by how long ago each was last asked for: P (longest ago), Q, R (most recent). Step 1 - request for P: P is in the cache, so by p1 this is a hit; p2 states 'a hit counts as an asking, so a record that is found in the cache is thereby moved to the back of the queue for eviction'. New order, oldest asking first: Q, R, P. Step 2 - request for S: S is not held, so it is a miss; the cache holds three records and already holds three, so by p1 'if the cache is full one record must be dropped'. p2's rule drops 'whichever record has gone longest without being asked for', which is now Q. Resulting order after admission: R, P, S. Answer: Q. On the specific point being checked - the pack's stated treatment of a hit DOES change the answer. Delete the second sentence of p2 and the natural reading is that only misses re-order the queue, leaving P as the record that has gone longest without being asked for and making option (a) correct. Option (a) is exactly the answer you get if you ignore that sentence, so the item is load-bearing on it rather than decorative. Option (d) contradicts p1: the cache is full at three records, so something must be dropped regardless of the earlier hit. Option (c) names the most recently asked-for record, the opposite of the rule. The pack's own rule leads cleanly to an option that is present, and the traced answer looks right. Full ablation (Claude Opus 5): not-determinable without the pack (would have chosen "b", confidence low) — I cannot answer this from general computing knowledge alone; the answer turns on a convention the stem never states. The stem says 'According to the policy' but names no policy, and more than one standard replacement policy is consistent with the facts given. Recency after the hit is Q (oldest), R, P (newest). LRU evicts Q (option b). MRU evicts P (option a). FIFO evicts by insertion order, which the stem never gives — if insertion happened to match the stated order it evicts P (option a), since a hit does not reorder a FIFO queue. LFU gives P two accesses and Q and R one each, leaving a Q/R tie that needs a tiebreak rule the stem also does not supply, so under LFU even option c is reachable. Option d is eliminable on general grounds: the S request is a miss into a full three-record cache, so something must be evicted regardless of policy, and the earlier P hit is irrelevant to that. So general knowledge gets me from four options to three, and the remaining choice is exactly the thing the source pack supplies. I choose b on two weak, non-domain grounds only: LRU is by far the most common policy a short passage would state, and the item's own construction supplies recency data and stages a deliberate re-access, which is informative only under a recency-updating policy. That is test-taking inference about how the item was built, not knowledge of what the source says, so I record the verdict as not-determinable with low confidence.

Hit rate is a property of a workload met by a cache, not an intrinsic property of the cache design: a cache fronting a skewed, repetitive request stream posts a high hit rate that says nothing about how it would perform on someone else's traffic, so cross-deployment hit rates do not rank designs. That is option b, and it is the well-known objection. Option a is wrong because equalising request counts does not equalise request mixes, which is the actual confound. Option c is wrong on its face: differing capacities are one reason the comparison is not apples to apples but they do not make ratios incomparable as figures, and it also misdiagnoses the problem as arithmetic rather than as workload dependence. Option d overreaches with 'too short a period to be used at all' — a one-day measurement is a weak basis for extrapolation but is not useless, and blanket dismissals of that form are rarely what a source text argues.
